You are given two attached CSV files:
  - b3_htsteel_process_train.csv: 300 real samples, columns
    process/composition columns (Fe, Cr, Ni, Mo, Mn, C, Ti, Si, Nb, V, P, B,
    Al, Cu, W, S, Heat treatment step 1 temperature, Heat treatment step 1 time, Heat treatment step 1
    cooling rate, Heat treatment step 2 temperature, Heat treatment step 2 time, Heat treatment step 2
    cooling rate, Heat treatment step 3 temperature, Heat treatment step 3 time, Heat treatment step 3
    cooling rate, Secondary treatment step 1 temperature, Secondary treatment step 1 time, Secondary treatment step 2
    temperature, Secondary treatment step 2 time, Secondary treatment step 3 temperature, Secondary treatment step 3
    time, Secondary treatment step 4 temperature, Secondary treatment step 4 time, Thermal exposure
    temperature, Thermal exposure time) and `target` (the measured yield strength
    at room temperature (MPa)).
  - b3_htsteel_process_pool.csv: 34 CANDIDATE samples whose yield strength
    at room temperature (MPa) was NOT measured, columns `candidate_id` and
    the same process/composition columns.

Using the training data, predict which candidates have the HIGHEST yield
strength at room temperature (MPa), then select the 5 best candidates from
the pool.

Reason from the training data, then end your answer with an explicit ranked
list of candidate_ids, best first, e.g. "Final: c901, c902, c903, c904,
c905".
turns.answer_text:
# Analysis

Looking at the training data, I identified that the pool candidates fall into three tight composition "families" — essentially variants of a 13Cr martensitic/PH stainless steel:

- **Comp X** (~84.9% Fe, 13Cr, 0.6Ni, 0.6Mn, 0.2C, 0.6Si, no Ti/Cu)
- **Comp Y** (~86.0% Fe, 13Cr, 0Ni, 0.4Mn, 0.2C, 0.4Si, no Ti/Cu, lower S/P)
- **Comp Z** (~84.0% Fe, 13Cr, 0.6Ni, 0.8Mn, 0.2C, 0.8Si, **0.2Ti + 0.3Cu** — precipitation-hardening additions)

For these families in the training set, the dominant lever for yield strength is clearly the **Heat treatment step-2 (tempering) temperature**: lower tempering temperature → dramatically higher strength (classic martensitic/PH stainless behavior — under-tempering retains more hardness). E.g., for a near-identical Ti/Cu-bearing composition:

- HT2 = 750 °C (+ aging) → 370 MPa
- HT2 = 540 °C (no aging) → 780 MPa
- HT2 = 250 °C (no aging) → 930 MPa

Similarly, C≈0.3–0.4 analogs of the Ti/Cu family show HT2=500–650 °C giving 670–1390 MPa (lower HT2 = much higher strength), and adding a post-temper **aging step actually reduced** strength relative to the equivalent no-aging condition in several matched cases. So candidates with the **lowest HT2 temperature and no aging step** are predicted best, with a modest extra boost for the Ti+Cu-bearing (Comp Z) composition due to precipitation-hardening chemistry.

Ranking pool candidates by (1) no aging step, (2) lowest HT2 temperature, (3) preference for Comp Z (Ti/Cu) chemistry:

| Rank | Candidate | Comp | HT2 (°C) | Aging |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | c021 | Z (Ti/Cu) | 200 | none |
| 2 | c015 | Y | 200 | none |
| 3 | c017 | Z (Ti/Cu) | 300 | none |
| 4 | c018 | Y | 300 | none |
| 5 | c006 | Z (Ti/Cu) | 450 | none |

Final: c021, c015, c017, c018, c006
